name: Chemical Physics

papers.title: Dressed Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory: Opening and Closing a Pandora's box
papers.abstract: Dressed time-dependent density functional theory (DTDDFT) has been shown to overcome the inability of adiabatic TDDFT to describe excitation energies and oscillator strengths of double-excitation character, however, it is far from being a black-box method. Here, we outline and address several operational issues while benchmarking the approach on a range of molecules. We define a protocol to determine whether an excitation from adiabatic TDDFT needs a double-excitation correction, without requiring a priori knowledge of the state, and which Kohn-Sham states to build the frequency-dependent DTDDFT matrix from. We present an 'undownfolding' that replaces this frequency-dependent matrix by a linear frequency-independent one in a larger space, eliminating ambiguities in the iterative procedure required to diagonalize the former. We compare the performance of DTDDFT for both excitation energies and oscillator strengths, as measured by an approximate metric for their single-excitation character, for different choices of the underlying adiabatic density functional approximation, with and without employing the Tamm-Dancoff approximation, for molecular excitations predicted by wavefunction methods to have either partial or genuine double-excitation character. We propose a correction to DTDDFT to account for missing dynamical correlation that is removed in the truncation procedure inherent in the method, and discuss the possibility of unphysical imaginary frequencies reminiscent of the 'triplet instability' that may arise. We provide benchmark data for butadiene, hexatriene, octatetraene, cyclopentadiene, acrolein, naphthalene, ethylene, borole, and cyclopentadienone. In some cases, DTDDFT predicts frequencies with about as much accuracy as the same underlying adiabatic TDDFT predicts for the constituent and near-lying single excitations.

papers.title: Computing hydration free energies and crystalline solubility of drug-like molecules with MACE
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of thermodynamic solubility is critical in drug discovery, where it influences oral bioavailability and drives decisions in formulation chemistry. First-principles calculations of intrinsic solubility offer the potential to achieve superior generalization to existing direct, data-driven predictors, which often suffer significant performance degradation outside of their training distribution. Whilst free energy perturbation calculations provide a rigorous framework to estimate these quantities, their accuracy is typically limited by the quality of the empirical force field used. In this work, we present a computational workflow driven by the MACE family of machine learning interatomic potentials to compute the solubility of neutral drug-like molecules. We introduce $\lambda$-MACE, a potential optimised for condensed-phase free energy calculations, which enables hydration free energy calculations at experimental accuracy on an evaluation set of 70 compounds from the FreeSolv database selected for their relevance to medicinal chemistry. We further combine these hydration free energy calculations with sublimation free energy calculations to predict crystalline solubility given a known experimental crystal structure, on an additional set of 10 compounds. We achieve state-of-the-art performance for each leg of the calculation, with experimental accuracy for the hydration leg, and accuracy competitive with industry-standard DFT for the sublimation leg. However, the overall errors after combining both legs lead to accuracy of 1.53 log units. This is significantly above the experimental accuracy (0.17-0.6 log units). Closing this gap will require substantially tighter accuracy in each leg, on the order of half of chemical accuracy (0.5 kcal/mol), with crystalline thermodynamics the hardest remaining challenge.

papers.title: Analytic sc$GW$ nuclear gradients with the resolution-of-identity approximation
papers.abstract: We present the first fully analytic derivation and implementation of nuclear gradients for the finite-temperature sc$GW$ method. The derivation is formulated within the $\Phi$-derivable framework of sc$GW$, using a Lagrangian formulation to obtain the analytic gradients. With the resolution-of-identity approximation, the computational cost of evaluating the gradients scales as $O(N_{\tau}N_\text{aux}^{2}N_\text{AO}^{2})$, exhibiting the same asymptotic scaling as the parent sc$GW$ method. Using the newly implemented analytic gradients, we perform geometry optimizations for several molecular systems and benchmark the resulting structures against those obtained with Hartree--Fock, $G_{0}W_{0}$, MP2, CCSD, and CCSD(T). We find that sc$GW$ generally yields reasonable molecular geometries, with its performance being comparable to that of CCSD for several systems. Overall, these results demonstrate the potential of analytic sc$GW$ gradients for reliable geometry optimizations for molecular systems while retaining the favorable $O(N_{\tau}N_\text{aux}^{2}N_\text{AO}^2)$ scaling of the underlying method.

papers.title: OrbACE: Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion
papers.abstract: Accurate electronic-structure reference data are expensive, motivating interatomic potentials that learn effectively from limited training sets. We introduce OrbACE (Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion), a framework that supplements an E(3)-equivariant cluster-expansion backbone with inexpensive electronic-structure descriptors. On ANI-1x at the $\omega$B97X/6-31G* level, its atom-centered variant, OrbACE-A, trained on 10,000 configurations and evaluated on 442,000 held-out configurations, achieves energy and force mean absolute errors of 3.16 meV/atom and 76 meV/angstrom in direct learning, compared with 9.61 meV/atom and 146 meV/angstrom for MACE with matched backbone settings. This reduces the energy error by a factor of three and approximately halves the force error. Its energy error is also below that of the best delta-corrected MACE baseline, 5.00 meV/atom, although its force error is slightly higher. Combining OrbACE-A with a Hartree-Fock delta baseline further reduces the errors to 1.48 meV/atom and 35 meV/angstrom. OrbACE-A builds atom- and pair-resolved invariants from a non-self-consistent extended-Hueckel model evaluated within the differentiable forward pass, yielding forces consistent with the predicted energy. The orbital variant, OrbACE-O, instead uses localized Hartree-Fock orbitals as graph nodes, with scalar and equivariant electronic descriptors. Its forces are evaluated at fixed descriptors, omitting their response to nuclear motion. In direct learning on ANI-1x, its energy error is approximately three times that of OrbACE-A. The three benchmarks considered (ANI-1x, revised MD17, and 3BPA) cover neutral, closed-shell, non-periodic molecules containing H, C, N, and O. Performance outside this domain remains to be established.

papers.title: Geometry Sets the Neutral MLIP-DFT Gap in Non-Covalent Binding, and Charged Systems Fail
papers.abstract: Pretrained universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are widely expected to substitute for explicit quantum chemistry when screening molecular interactions. On non-covalent binding we find that this expectation holds for neutral chemistry and fails for charged chemistry. We audit the FAIRChem UMA OMol head, without task-specific fine-tuning, on 5,567 probe-target dimers from 18 benchmarks across nine fidelity arms, using RAPIDS (Rapid Atomistic Probe-target Interaction Discovery Scaffold), a training-free inference-time scaffold. First, on neutral chemistry RAPIDS reaches a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.37 kcal/mol, matching or beating every explicit DFT single-point fidelity (1.42-1.50 kcal/mol), so the remaining MLIP-DFT gap is geometric rather than a learned-surface error. Second, charged systems form a qualitatively different regime: MAE jumps to 8.5-22.9 kcal/mol across three charged benchmarks; DFT single-point rescoring does not restore accuracy, geometry reoptimization restores it for ionic hydrogen bonds and ion-molecule dimers, and the failure persists across all three MLIP backbones. Third, the residual failures are structured: signed biases cluster by chemistry family, and whether a fidelity fails catastrophically transfers across families more reliably than error magnitude, enabling cost-aware fidelity selection. RAPIDS-Select, a closed-form rule on cheap precomputed features, uses about 37% less compute than a strong static DFT baseline at matched accuracy, and on a newly computed charged benchmark cuts the catastrophe rate from 68% to 5.7%. On WetSenseBench, a wet-lab-grounded host-guest selectivity benchmark from eight sensing studies, RAPIDS without DFT follow-up recovers 82.9% pair-level agreement on the seven studies above its ~1 kcal/mol precision floor.

papers.title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
papers.abstract: Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation. We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

papers.title: Bringing Singles to $GW$: A Coupled-Cluster Perspective on Orbital Relaxation
papers.abstract: The one-shot $G_0W_0$ approximation suffers from a pronounced dependence on the underlying mean-field starting point. Here, we explore an alternative to conventional self-consistent $GW$ schemes by introducing single excitations within the recently established connection between $GW$ and extended coupled-cluster (ECC) theory. Starting from the equivalence between $G_0W_0$ and ionization-potential/electron-affinity equation-of-motion direct-ring extended coupled-cluster doubles (IP/EA-EOM-drECCD), we extend the formalism to include right-hand single-excitation and left-hand single-deexcitation cluster amplitudes coupled to the direct-ring doubles amplitudes. The resulting approximation, denoted singles-$G_0W_0$ (s$G_0W_0$), incorporates orbital-relaxation effects without explicitly introducing self-consistency in the Green's function. We assess the performance of s$G_0W_0$ for molecular valence and core ionization potentials using Hartree-Fock and Kohn-Sham starting points. For both types of ionizations, the inclusion of singles largely suppresses the starting-point dependence observed in conventional $G_0W_0$, yielding quasiparticle energies close to those obtained from the Hartree-Fock reference, irrespective of the initial mean-field description. Although this does not necessarily translate into improved absolute accuracy, it demonstrates that singles provide an effective route to reducing the starting-point dependence of $GW$-like approximations without resorting to self-consistency.

papers.title: PineIR: 3D molecular structures from an infrared spectrum alone
papers.abstract: Computing the infrared (IR) spectrum of a molecule from its structure is routine. The inverse problem is not. In practice, IR spectra are used to identify the functional groups present in a molecule, while the determination of its complete structure requires additional measurements. Machine-learning models that return 3D structures from IR spectra exist, but all of them need extra input, such as Raman, ultraviolet or nuclear magnetic resonance spectra, the molecular formula, or the number of atoms. In this work we present PineIR, a generative model that returns 3D molecular structures from the IR spectrum alone. PineIR builds the molecule atom by atom, and each atom is associated with its contribution to the IR spectrum. This contribution is subtracted from the input spectrum before the next atom is generated. To train it, we computed with a machine-learned interatomic potential the IR spectra of 4.6 million structures of 3.1 million molecules, including conformer ensembles. On computed spectra of held-out molecules, the best-ranked of fifty candidates has the correct connectivity in 43% of the cases, and the generated geometries reproduce the conformer and the diastereomer that produced the input spectrum. After fine-tuning on 161k spectra calculated with the hybrid functional B3LYP, the model can also be applied to spectra at this level of theory.

papers.title: Automatic dual basis sets for self-consistent field calculations
papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) has long been the workhorse of electronic structure theory, and it is experiencing a new boom thanks to big data applications and machine learning. A DFT calculation requires the iterative solution of the self-consistent field (SCF) problem, whose cost is the product of (i) the number of SCF steps and (ii) the cost of a single step. The number of SCF steps depends strongly on the initial guess, regardless of the SCF algorithm, and quantitative DFT accuracy is known to require at least a polarized triple-$\zeta$ basis set. However, a qualitatively correct solution may often be found already in a smaller \emph{dual basis} (DB), which can then bootstrap a calculation in the full basis set. Traditionally, the DB is chosen by hand for each application to enable robust convergence to the ground state. In this work, we pursue automatic generation of DBs for SCF calculations. Our generator constructs a pruned orbital basis from the target orbital basis for a predefined precision threshold and a given Fock matrix. As expected, the larger the basis set is, the smaller the fraction of kept basis functions. The DBs produced by our algorithm exhibit similar performance for a wide range of systems from the first 4 periods of the periodic table. Ultimately, we find that presently available initial guesses for the Fock matrix are not accurate enough to unlock the use of adaptive basis sets, and believe that the same limitation may hold for similar attempts for basis compactification.

papers.title: A general-purpose electron density model for molecular chemistry
papers.abstract: Universal machine-learning potentials predict molecular structure and stability at the accuracy of quantum mechanics, for a fraction of the cost. Properties derived instead from knowledge of the electronic structure give profound insights into chemical reactivity, but are not accessible with the same ease or transferability. We train PET-rho-OMol25, a model of the ground-state electron density and spin polarization of molecular systems on four million OMol25 structures in multiple charge and spin states. The model makes predictions for entire proteins in a few seconds on a single GPU, and enables estimation of important diagnostics of molecular structure and reactivity, such as vibrational Stark measurements, halogen $\sigma$-holes, hydrogen-bond basicities and core-level shifts, as well as spin density for redox chemistry and magnetism. PET-rho-OMol25 has an accuracy close to density-functional theory, with its least reliable predictions flagged by its built-in uncertainty estimator, for most properties and classes of compounds. It can be used as a drop-in replacement for electronic-structure calculations of the density, making insightful analyses available for larger and more complex structures.

papers.title: On the binding and stability of CeO2 molecules on low-index Au surfaces
papers.abstract: Many multi-phase thin films grown by self-assembly involve co-deposition of both metallic and oxide phases that grow into the same film. Under such conditions, the oxide species may be present in stoichiometric molecular form on the surface of the metallic phase. Quantifying the stability, binding, and diffusion of such molecular oxide states on metallic surfaces is critical for understanding self-assembly. In this work, we investigate the binding and stability of CeO2 molecules on Au surfaces using spin-polarized density functional theory calculations. Specifically, we examine how the configuration of the CeO2 molecule, its binding energy and binding free energy, structural stability, effective charge, and projected electronic density of states vary among various binding sites on Au(001), Au(110), and Au(111) surfaces. Molecular CeO2 was found to be more favorable on all Au surfaces than its atomic constituents. It was also found that the bent CeO2 molecule configuration is more stable than the linear counterpart, with the Ce atom on the hollow site and the O atoms on the top sites. In addition, the configurations of the CeO2 molecule on Au surfaces with a binding energy around or weaker than -1 eV were found to have a low probability of existence above room temperature. Furthermore, the charge transfer was found to occur in such a way that the CeO2 molecule becomes polarized on all surfaces, but the polarization is stronger only for the strongly bonded states on Au(001) and Au(110) surfaces. Finally, three different cases of how the CeO2 molecule binds to Au(001), Au(110), and Au(111) were identified: case 1: chemisorption with symmetric bonds, case 2: chemisorption with asymmetric bonds, and case 3: physisorption with symmetric bonds. These three cases of CeO2 binding are present on Au(001) and Au(110), but only cases 2 and 3 occur on Au(111).

papers.title: Quantum chaotic signature in non-empirical ensemble of DNA base pairs
papers.abstract: The statistical study of many-body chaotic quantum systems would indicate important phenomena such as short-range level repulsion and long-range spectral rigidity. We investigate such behavior in an ensemble of gas-phase guanine-cytosine (GC) and adenine-thymine (AT) Watson-Crick (WC) base pairs by calculating their Kohn-Sham molecular orbital energy levels via ab initio density functional theory (DFT). We track the probability distribution, adjacent-gap ratios (AGR), number variance, and spectral compressibility of the unfolded level spacings to see whether their statistics follow the statistics of the eigenvalues of random matrices. After comparing the results to Poisson, semi-Poisson (SP), and Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) statistics, it becomes evident that the statistics of orbital energy levels agree closely with the semi-Poisson distribution, pointing to an intermediate regime between integrability and chaos, characterized by level repulsion and strong long-range correlations. Potential biophysical implications for charge transfer and related biological processes are also discussed.

papers.title: Spin-Orbit Coupling in Symmetry-Forbidden Reactions: A Selection Rule Tested on the Chalcogen Trimers
papers.abstract: A reaction is forbidden by orbital symmetry when an occupied and an empty orbital of different symmetry change places along its path. With spin-orbit coupling orbitals become spinors, and those of two such orbitals can mix only if the orbitals differ by the symmetry of a rotation; the operator component of that symmetry couples ground state and diradical triplet. We test this rule on the ring opening of the chalcogen trimers O3 to Po3, where an in-plane and an out-of-plane orbital cross ($C_{2v}$ surfaces; NEVPT2, spin-orbit configuration interaction), by letting the operator components act separately. In Se3 and Te3 the component named by the rule alone lowers the barrier by 2.2 and 5.1 kcal/mol (complete operator: 2.2 and 5.2), the other two by 0.2 and 1.3 kcal/mol; in Po3 they contribute in second order. The triplet crosses the ground state 6.5 to 9.0 kcal/mol below the forbidden saddle. Spin-orbit coupling makes this crossing passable in O3 and S3 and, from Se3 on, merges the two states into one surface whose saddle lies 2.6, 5.5, and 13.1 kcal/mol lower. Molecular rotation obeys the same rule but is 6 to $2.8\times 10^{3}$ times weaker, which bears on the lifetime predicted for cyclic ozone.

papers.title: Site-Resolved Optical Spectroscopy of Thulium in Solid Argon
papers.abstract: We utilize the high resolution of the ground state transition ${}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2} \leftrightarrow {}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}$ in thulium atoms isolated in solid argon to perform excitation-emission spectroscopy. Decomposition of the excitation-emission spectrum reveals 6 absorption-emission profiles, which are attributed to multiple trapping sites in the host matrix. Comparison with vacuum transition energies shows large matrix-induced shifts for $\mathrm{s}\rightarrow\mathrm{p}$ transitions, whereas $\mathrm{f} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ transitions remain close to their free-atom energies. A single site exhibiting strong emission at 560nm is investigated and a three-photon excitation pathway is determined as a possible origin of the high energy 560nm light. Additionally, for long-lived levels belonging to the $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ configuration, narrow, crystal-field split absorption lines are identified. Matrix effects are important for establishing the mechanism behind the observed spectra and long $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ lifetimes.

papers.title: Transition Path Sampling for Rare Events in Non-Markovian Open Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: Rare transitions govern the dynamics of many open quantum systems, but their probabilities and rates are difficult to calculate. Transition path sampling (TPS) of quantum systems has so far been limited to Markovian, perturbative descriptions. Here, we formulate TPS for non-Markovian quantum state diffusion, which is exact for Gaussian baths, extending it to non-Markovian and strongly coupled open quantum systems. For normal-to-superradiant tunneling in the unbalanced open Dicke model, we determine probabilities down to $10^{-8}$ and rates beyond the reach of brute force.
